title: Newborn blood spot and hearing screening
blurb: Offer the newborn blood spot test (day 5, 10 conditions) and the hearing screen, explain consent and declining rules, and know what happens after a no clear response result.
question: On day 5, Ama and Kofi agree to blood spot screening for sickle cell disease and cystic fibrosis but say they do not want their baby tested for PKU or MCADD. What can the midwife offer, and what should she explain?

teach.body: Formally: the NHS newborn blood spot (NBS) screening programme identifies babies with 10 rare but serious conditions so that treatment can start early, improving health and preventing severe disability or death. The newborn hearing screening programme aims to identify permanent moderate, severe and profound deafness. In plain English: a heel-prick card and a quick ear test catch conditions that look invisible at birth. Both are offered to every baby, and screening is always a choice.
teach.cite: NHS England NBS programme overview (updated 26 Sept 2025); NHSP overview

Conditions

teach.h: Offering the blood spot test well
items: Explain the purpose and give the 'Screening tests for you and your baby' leaflet (available in 13 languages and easy-read guides).
Ask for verbal consent and record what was accepted or declined.
Keep the baby warm and comfortable; feeding and cuddling help during the heel prick.
Follow sample-taking guidelines so the sample is good quality, and send it the same day.
Tell parents results come within 6 weeks, sooner if a condition is suspected.

steps.label: AOAE test
steps.sub: soft earpiece, clicking sounds; a few minutes

teach.caption: Offered to all babies, ideally within the first 4 weeks of life; can be done up to 3 months of age. Babies in neonatal intensive care follow a different pathway.

teach.h: A clear result is not a guarantee
teach.body: A clear hearing result makes hearing loss unlikely, but screening does not pick up all types, and hearing loss can develop later. Parents should use the checklist in the personal child health record (red book) and talk to the health visitor or GP with any concerns. Parents who decline the hearing screen are given checklists to help them check their baby's hearing as the baby grows.

Parents can decline SCD, CF and CHT individually, but the seven inherited metabolic diseases, which include PKU and MCADD, can be declined only as a group. The midwife explains this without pressure: if they decline PKU and MCADD they are declining all seven IMDs, including conditions such as MCADD where early detection can prevent sudden collapse. She records their decision clearly, and tells them they can change their mind up to their baby's first birthday.

teach.text: Day 5 counts the day of birth as DAY 0. A baby born on Monday has the sample on Saturday, not Friday. And cystic fibrosis screening is unreliable after 8 weeks, even though the other conditions can be screened up to 1 year.

items: Blood spot on day 5 (birth = day 0); 10 conditions; results within 6 weeks.
Decline SCD, CF and CHT individually; the 7 IMDs only as a group.
Eligible up to 1 year if missed; CF unreliable after 8 weeks.
Hearing: AOAE first, AABR if needed; can be done up to 3 months; no clear response means audiology within 4 weeks.
Screening is always a choice: verbal consent, recorded.

summary: You can now offer newborn blood spot and hearing screening, name the 10 blood spot conditions, and apply the declining rules. You can also time the blood spot sample correctly, explain results, and describe the hearing screen pathway after a no clear response result.

A.q: Baby Tia was born on a Wednesday. On which day should her blood spot sample usually be taken?
A.why: The sample is usually taken on day 5, with the day of birth counted as day 0. Wednesday is day 0, so day 5 is Monday.

whyNot.2: Sunday is day 4; it counts the day of birth as day 1.

A.q: How many conditions does the NHS newborn blood spot programme in England screen for after September 2025?
A.why: Since hereditary tyrosinaemia type 1 (HT1) was added in September 2025, NBS screens for 10 conditions.

whyNot.0: 9 was the number before HT1 was added in September 2025.
whyNot.2: 7 is the number of inherited metabolic diseases within the 10.

A.q: Which blood spot conditions can parents decline individually?
options: Sickle cell disease, CF and CHT
A.why: NBS programme: parents can decline SCD, CF and CHT individually but can decline the 7 IMDs only as a group.

whyNot.0: These are inherited metabolic diseases, which are declined as a group.
whyNot.1: The IMDs cannot be declined individually.
whyNot.3: HT1 is an IMD, so it cannot be declined separately from the other six.

B.q: Baby Jacob, born at home, did not have a blood spot test. He is now 10 weeks old and his family have just registered with a GP. Which statement is accurate?
options: He can be screened, but CF is unreliable now
He is too old for any blood spot screening
He can be screened for all 10 conditions reliably
He should wait until his first birthday
B.why: NBS programme: babies are eligible for blood spot screening up to their first birthday, except cystic fibrosis testing, which is unreliable after 8 weeks of age.

whyNot.1: Babies remain eligible up to 1 year old.
whyNot.2: CF screening is unreliable after 8 weeks, so not all 10 can be screened reliably.
whyNot.3: Waiting until 1 year would exceed eligibility and delay treatment.

B.q: By when should parents usually receive their baby's blood spot results?
B.why: NBS programme: parents receive the results within 6 weeks, sooner if a condition is suspected.

whyNot.0: Routine results are not available within 48 hours.
whyNot.1: 2 weeks is shorter than the stated routine timescale.
whyNot.3: Results come by 6 weeks, not at 1 year.

B.q: Baby Mila's hearing screen shows no clear response in her left ear after the AOAE test and repeat. What happens next?
options: Discharge with a hearing checklist now
Urgent ENT review the same day
B.why: If screening does not show a clear response in one or both ears, a referral for audiological assessment is made, to be seen within 4 weeks.

whyNot.0: Waiting until 6 to 8 weeks delays the audiology assessment.
whyNot.2: A checklist is given to parents who decline screening; a no clear response result needs referral.
whyNot.3: Same-day ENT review is not the hearing screening pathway.

C.q: Hana, 28, tells the midwife at booking that her first child has cystic fibrosis. What should happen regarding newborn blood spot screening?
options: Wait for the routine day 5 sample as usual
Skip CF screening because the risk is already known
Replace routine screening with a CF test at birth
Make a care plan, maybe with an early extra sample
C.why: NBS programme: ask about a family history of the NBS conditions during pregnancy; if present, create a care plan, which could include an additional early blood spot sample.

whyNot.0: A known family history needs a care plan made in pregnancy.
whyNot.1: The baby still needs screening; a known risk makes early testing more important.
whyNot.2: The care plan may add an early sample, but routine screening for all 10 conditions is still offered.

C.q: Grace and Sam decline newborn hearing screening for their baby. What should the midwife provide?
options: Checklists to check their baby's hearing
A referral to audiology at 4 weeks
A safeguarding referral for refusing screening
A letter saying hearing is normal
C.why: NHS: screening is a choice. Parents who decline are given checklists to help them check their baby's hearing as they grow, and can raise concerns with the health visitor or GP.

whyNot.1: Audiology referral follows a no clear response screen, not a decision to decline.
whyNot.2: Declining screening is a lawful choice and is not a safeguarding concern by itself.
whyNot.3: No screening has been done, so no result can be given.

C.q: On day 5, the midwife takes Baby Ivo's blood spot sample at a home visit at 16:00. What should happen to the card?
options: Post it the next working day
Keep it in the fridge until Monday
Send it to the laboratory the same day
Hand it to the parents to take to the GP
C.why: NBS programme: samples should be sent to the screening laboratory for analysis the same day they are taken, to avoid delays in diagnosing time-critical conditions such as MCADD.

whyNot.1: Holding samples delays analysis and is not the standard.
whyNot.3: The professional is responsible for sending the sample to the laboratory.

reteach.title: Five days, ten conditions, six weeks
reteach.question: Most blood spot questions turn on three numbers. What are they, and what do they mean?

blocks.body: DAY 5: the usual day for the heel prick, counting the day of birth as day 0. TEN conditions: SCD, CF, CHT plus 7 inherited metabolic diseases (PKU, MCADD, MSUD, IVA, GA1, homocystinuria, HT1). SIX weeks: when parents receive results. Add two limits: eligible up to 1 year, but CF unreliable after 8 weeks.

blocks.text: The 7 IMDs are all-or-nothing: parents cannot accept PKU but decline MCADD.

explain.body: Sickle cell disease, cystic fibrosis, congenital hypothyroidism, and 7 inherited metabolic diseases: PKU, MCADD, MSUD, IVA, GA1, homocystinuria and HT1 (added Sept 2025).

test.q: Which condition was added to the blood spot programme in September 2025?
test.why: NBS programme overview (updated 26 Sept 2025): hereditary tyrosinaemia type 1 (HT1) was added to the list of IMDs screened for.

whyNot.0: Spinal muscular atrophy is not one of the 10 national NBS conditions listed by the programme.
whyNot.2: Galactosaemia is not one of the 10 NBS conditions.
whyNot.3: Biotinidase deficiency is not one of the 10 NBS conditions.

explain.body: Usually day 5, counting the day of birth as day 0. Send the sample the same day. Results within 6 weeks. Eligible up to 1 year if missed; CF unreliable after 8 weeks.

test.q: After what age is blood spot screening for cystic fibrosis considered unreliable?
test.why: NBS programme: CF testing is unreliable after 8 weeks of age.

whyNot.0: 2 weeks is too early a limit.
whyNot.1: 6 weeks is the results timescale, not the CF limit.
whyNot.2: 1 year is the eligibility limit for the other conditions.

explain.body: Verbal consent, recorded. Parents can decline SCD, CF and CHT individually; the 7 IMDs can be declined only as a group. Give the 'Screening tests for you and your baby' leaflet.

test.q: What type of consent is sought for newborn blood spot screening?
test.why: NBS programme: parents are asked for verbal consent for newborn blood spot screening, which is recorded.

whyNot.1: Written consent is not required for NBS.
whyNot.2: Attendance alone does not imply consent; parents are asked.
whyNot.3: Consent is given by the parents, not the GP.

explain.body: Offered to all babies, ideally within the first 4 weeks; can be done up to 3 months. AOAE (earpiece, clicks) first; some babies need AABR (3 sensors, headphones, 5 to 15 minutes). No clear response in one or both ears: audiology referral within 4 weeks.
explain.cite: NHSP overview; NHS Newborn hearing screening

test.q: Up to what age can the newborn hearing screen be carried out?
test.why: NHS: newborn hearing screening is usually offered before the baby is 4 weeks old, but it can be done up to 3 months of age (also NHSP overview).

whyNot.0: 6 weeks is shorter than the upper age limit.
whyNot.1: 1 year is the blood spot eligibility limit, not the hearing screen.
whyNot.3: 72 hours is the NIPE newborn examination deadline.
